items.followUp: Define equilibrium and explain its second condition, giving one example.

rubric.why: Checks that the definition includes both force and rotational balance.
rubric.description: Defines equilibrium as having zero resultant force and zero resultant torque.
rubric.how: State that both the net force and net torque on the body are zero.

rubric.why: Checks that an example of a body in equilibrium is given.
rubric.how: Name a book resting on a table or another valid equilibrium example.

rubric.why: Checks the statement of the first condition of equilibrium.
rubric.description: States that the vector sum of forces is zero.
rubric.how: Write the first condition as the vector sum of all forces being zero.

rubric.why: Checks an example showing how forces can balance under the first condition.
rubric.description: Gives an example of balanced forces.
rubric.how: Describe equal and opposite forces, such as a body's weight balanced by an upward force.

modelAnswer: A body is in equilibrium when the resultant force and the resultant torque acting on it are both zero.
For example, a book resting on a table is in equilibrium.
The first condition of equilibrium is that the vector sum of all forces acting on a body is zero: ΣF = 0.
For example, equal forces acting in opposite directions balance each other; a book's weight downward is balanced by the table's upward force.

items.followUp: An object weighs 24 N in air and 15 N when fully immersed in water. Calculate its density. Take the density of water as 1000 kg/m³.

rubric.why: Checks that the given weights and the assumed density of water are identified for the calculation.
rubric.description: Identifies the weights in air and water and the density of water.
rubric.how: Record 18 N in air, 11.4 N in water, and use 1000 kg/m³ for water.

rubric.why: Checks that the loss of weight in water is correctly calculated.
rubric.description: Calculates the loss in weight as 6.6 N.
rubric.how: Subtract the immersed weight from the weight in air.

rubric.why: Checks that the density relationship using loss of weight is used.
rubric.description: Writes the density formula based on weight in air and loss of weight.

rubric.why: Checks correct substitution of the given values into the density formula.
rubric.description: Substitutes the weights and water density into the formula.

rubric.why: Checks the calculated density and its unit.
rubric.description: Gives the object's density with a suitable unit.
rubric.how: Report approximately 2.73 × 10³ kg/m³, or an equivalent density.

modelAnswer: Given: Weight in air, Wair = 18 N; weight in water, Wwater = 11.4 N; density of water, ρwater = 1000 kg/m³.
Loss in weight = Wair − Wwater = 18 N − 11.4 N = 6.6 N.
